i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0:12

t: Shout their name, tap their shoulder.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0:13

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0:17
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Postpartum Hemorrhage (Severe Bleeding After Birth) Postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) is the leading cause of maternal death worldwide.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0:18
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: It occurs when the mother bleeds heavily after delivering the baby.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0:19
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Heavy bleeding can kill within 2 hours if not controlled.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0:20
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: SIGNS & SYMPTOMS Soaking more than one large cloth or pad per 15 minutes Blood pooling rapidly beneath the mother Mother feels faint, dizzy, or confused Pale, cold, clammy skin Rapid, weak pulse (heart beating very fast but faintly) Uterus (belly

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:0
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: bleeding can kill within 2 hours if not controlled.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:1
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: SIGNS & SYMPTOMS Soaking more than one large cloth or pad per 15 minutes Blood pooling rapidly beneath the mother Mother feels faint, dizzy, or confused Pale, cold, clammy skin Rapid, weak pulse (heart beating very fast but faintly) Uterus (belly below navel) feels soft and floppy instead of firm IMMEDIATE ACTIONS DO THESE IN ORDER 6.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:2
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: MASSAGE THE UTERUS: Place one hand flat on the lower belly, just below the navel.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:3
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Press down firmly and rub in a circular motion.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:4
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: The uterus should harden like a ball under your hand within 12 minutes.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:5
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: This is the single most important action.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:6
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Continue until it stays firm.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:7
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: PUT THE BABY TO BREAST: If the baby is able, place it to the mother's breast to suckle immediately.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:8
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Breastfeeding causes the body to release hormones that contract the uterus and reduce bleeding.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:9
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Do this even while massaging.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:10
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: CONTROL EXTERNAL BLEEDING: Pack clean cloths tightly against any visible bleeding wound from delivery tears.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:11
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Apply direct firm pressure.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:12
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Do not remove cloths add more on top if soaked.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:13
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: KEEP HER WARM: Cover the mother with any available cloth or blanket.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:14
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: ELEVATE HER LEGS: If she is dizzy or unresponsive, lay her flat and raise her legs above the level of her heart using rolled clothing or bags.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:15
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: This pushes blood toward vital organs.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:16
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: DO NOT LEAVE HER ALONE: Stay with her and monitor continuously.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:17
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If bleeding does not slow within 15 minutes of uterus massage, she is in severe danger.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:18
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Begin evacuation to any medical facility immediately while continuing care.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:19
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: [Page 4] Ongoing Care Continue uterine massage every 510 minutes to ensure the uterus stays firm Encourage oral fluids (water, broth) if she is conscious and not vomiting Track her pulse: press two fingers on the inside of her wrist.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:20
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: More than 100 beats per minute is alarming.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:21
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: More than 120 is critical.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:22
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Keep her calm and reassured fear increases blood loss What NOT to Do Do NOT pull on the umbilical cord to deliver the placenta.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:23
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: This can cause life- threatening hemorrhage and uterine inversion.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:24
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Do NOT give the mother alcohol.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:25
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Do NOT leave the placenta inside without medical help beyond 1 hour post- delivery.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:26
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Eclampsia (Seizures During or After Pregnancy) Eclampsia is a dangerous condition where a pregnant or recently delivered woman has seizures due

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:0
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: can cause life- threatening hemorrhage and uterine inversion.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:1
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Do NOT give the mother alcohol.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:2
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Do NOT leave the placenta inside without medical help beyond 1 hour post- delivery.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:3
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Eclampsia (Seizures During or After Pregnancy) Eclampsia is a dangerous condition where a pregnant or recently delivered woman has seizures due to very high blood pressure.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:4
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: It can occur up to 6 weeks after delivery.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:5
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: SIGNS & SYMPTOMS Sudden seizure (shaking, convulsions, loss of consciousness) Before the seizure: severe headache, blurred vision, swelling of face/hands She may be unresponsive after the seizure for several minutes Confusion or unusual behavior after a seizure IMMEDIATE ACTIONS 12.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:6
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: PROTECT HER FROM INJURY: Clear the area around her of hard objects.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:7
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Do not put anything in her mouth.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:8
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: POSITION: Turn her gently onto her left side during and after the seizure (recovery position).

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:9
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: This keeps her airway clear and reduces pressure on major blood vessels.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:10
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: TIME THE SEIZURE: Note when it starts.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:11
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: A seizure lasting more than 5 minutes is a medical emergency.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:12
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: AFTER THE SEIZURE: Keep her on her left side.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:13
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Talk to her calmly as she regains consciousness.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:14
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: EVACUATE IMMEDIATELY: Eclampsia requires urgent hospital care.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:15
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: This is a life- threatening condition.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:16
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: [Page 5] Do NOT put fingers or objects in her mouth.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:17
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: You will be bitten and it does not help her.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:18
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Newborn Not Breathing at Birth Most babies who do not cry immediately after birth can be resuscitated with basic stimulation.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:19
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Reference: WHO Basic Newborn Resuscitation (2012).

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:20
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: IMMEDIATE ACTIONS FIRST 60 SECONDS ARE CRITICAL 17.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:21
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: DRY AND WARM: Immediately wrap the baby in a dry cloth.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:22
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Rub the back and soles of feet vigorously for 30 seconds.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:23
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: This stimulates breathing.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:24
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: CLEAR THE AIRWAY: Wipe the mouth and nose with a clean cloth.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:25
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Do not suction unless you have a bulb syringe.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:26
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: POSITION: Lay the baby flat on its back with the head in a neutral position (not tilted back, not chin on chest).

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:27
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Place a small roll under the shoulders.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:28
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: CHECK BREATHING: Watch for chest rise.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:29
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If breathing: keep warm, give to mother for skin-to-skin contact.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:30
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If NOT breathing after 30 seconds of stimulation: begin rescue breaths.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:31
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: RESCUE BREATHS: Cover both the baby's mouth AND nose with your mouth.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:32
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Give 5 small, gentle puffs just enough to see the chest

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:0
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If breathing: keep warm, give to mother for skin-to-skin contact.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:1
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If NOT breathing after 30 seconds of stimulation: begin rescue breaths.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:2
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: RESCUE BREATHS: Cover both the baby's mouth AND nose with your mouth.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:3
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Give 5 small, gentle puffs just enough to see the chest rise slightly.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:4
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Then give 1 breath every 3 seconds (20 per minute).

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:5
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Check again for breathing.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:6
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: IF NO PULSE: If the baby is not breathing and you cannot feel a heartbeat by pressing 2 fingers on the center of the chest, begin CPR: 3 chest compressions (pressing down about 1.5 cm with 2 fingers on the breastbone) followed by 1 breath.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:7
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: A baby that is limp and blue but warm still has a chance.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:8
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Babies can be resuscitated for several minutes after birth.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:9
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Newborn Hypothermia (Baby Getting Too Cold) Newborns lose heat extremely rapidly, especially in cold or damp environments.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:10
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Hypothermia is a leading preventable cause of newborn death in field conditions.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:11
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: SIGNS THE BABY IS TOO COLD IF: Skin is cold to touch on belly or back Lethargic, not feeding, not crying Blue or purple lips and fingernails [Page 6] Breathing slowly or weakly IMMEDIATE ACTIONS 23.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:12
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: SKIN-TO-SKIN: Place the baby directly on the mother's bare chest, between her breasts.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:13
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Cover both with a blanket.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:14
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: This is called kangaroo care and is the most effective rewarming method available without equipment.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:15
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: COVER THE HEAD: The baby loses most heat through the head.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:16
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Wrap or cover it immediately.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:17
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: KEEP ENVIRONMENT WARM: Move away from wind, rain, or cold surfaces.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:18
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Use body heat from any available adult if the mother is unable.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:19
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: FEED: If baby can suckle, breastfeed immediately.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:20
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Feeding provides calories and warmth.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:21
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: REASSESS: After 30 minutes of skin-to-skin contact, the baby should be warmer, pinker, and more active.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:22
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Retained Placenta (Placenta Not Delivered) Source: WHO Guidelines for the Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage and Retained Placenta (2009); MSF Obstetrics in Remote Settings.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:23
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: After the baby is born, the placenta (afterbirth) should normally deliver within 30 minutes.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:24
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If it does not come out, it is called a retained placenta.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:25
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: This is a leading cause of postpartum hemorrhage and requires urgent care.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:26
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: SIGNS Placenta has not delivered 3060 minutes after the baby was born Continued moderate bleeding despite a firm uterus Mother feels continued cramping or fullness in

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:0
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If it does not come out, it is called a retained placenta.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:1
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: This is a leading cause of postpartum hemorrhage and requires urgent care.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:2
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: SIGNS Placenta has not delivered 3060 minutes after the baby was born Continued moderate bleeding despite a firm uterus Mother feels continued cramping or fullness in the lower belly IMMEDIATE ACTIONS 28.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:3
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: DO NOT PULL THE CORD: Never pull, tug, or yank the umbilical cord to try to remove the placenta.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:4
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: This is the most dangerous mistake a bystander can make.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:5
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: It can cause uterine inversion (see 1F) and massive fatal hemorrhage.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:6
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: CONTINUE UTERUS MASSAGE: Keep massaging the lower belly to keep the uterus contracted and minimize bleeding.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:7
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: ENCOURAGE BREASTFEEDING: Put the baby to breast.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:8
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Natural hormones released during suckling help the uterus contract and may help expel the placenta.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:9
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: KEEP HER UPRIGHT: If able, help her squat or sit upright gravity may assist.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:10
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: MONITOR BLEEDING: If bleeding increases significantly, treat as postpartum hemorrhage (see 1A).

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:11
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: EVACUATE: Retained placenta beyond 60 minutes requires manual removal by a trained provider.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:12
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Begin evacuation while continuing care.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:13
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Do NOT attempt to manually remove the placenta without medical training.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:14
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Do NOT pull the cord under any circumstances.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:15
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Uterine Inversion (Uterus Turned Inside Out) Source: ICRC War Surgery; MSF Emergency Obstetric Care.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:16
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Uterine inversion is a rare but immediately life-threatening emergency, most commonly caused by pulling the umbilical cord too hard.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:17
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: The uterus partially or completely turns inside out through the vaginal opening.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:18
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: SIGNS RECOGNIZE IMMEDIATELY Sudden massive bleeding immediately after delivery A dark red mass visible at or protruding from the vaginal opening Mother goes into shock almost instantly pale, collapsed, unresponsive Severe pain OR no pain at all (if the mother is already in shock) FIELD ACTIONS 34.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:19
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: DO NOT ATTEMPT TO PUSH IT BACK IN: Without training and sterile conditions, attempting to replace the uterus causes further injury and infection.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:20
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: COVER WITH CLEAN DAMP CLOTH: Place the cleanest available damp cloth gently over the exposed tissue to protect it from drying out and contamination.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:21
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: LAY HER FLAT: Elevate her legs.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:22
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: She will be in severe shock.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:23
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: KEEP WARM: Cover her completely.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:24
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: EVACUATE IMMEDIATELY: This is a surgical emergency.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:25
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: She will die without intervention.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:26
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: This is the highest evacuation priority.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:27
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Uterine inversion is caused by pulling the umbilical cord.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:0
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: LAY HER FLAT: Elevate her legs.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:1
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: She will be in severe shock.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:2
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: KEEP WARM: Cover her completely.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:3
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: EVACUATE IMMEDIATELY: This is a surgical emergency.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:4
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: She will die without intervention.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:5
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: This is the highest evacuation priority.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:6
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Uterine inversion is caused by pulling the umbilical cord.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:7
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: This is why cord traction must never be performed by untrained persons.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:8
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Birth Canal Tears (Vaginal and Perineal Lacerations) Source: WHO Managing Complications in Pregnancy and Childbirth (2017).

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:9
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: [Page 8] Tears to the vaginal opening and perineum (area between vagina and anus) are very common after delivery, especially first deliveries.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:10
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: They cause continuous bleeding that is separate from uterine bleeding.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:11
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: SIGNS Continuous slow or moderate bleeding from below, even when the uterus feels firm and contracted Blood flows steadily rather than in gushes Visible wound or tear around the vaginal opening Mother reports sharp pain in the perineal area IMMEDIATE ACTIONS 39.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:12
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: APPLY DIRECT PRESSURE: Place a clean folded cloth firmly against the bleeding area and hold steady pressure.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:13
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Ask the mother to squeeze her thighs together if able to help maintain pressure.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:14
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: HOLD FOR 10 MINUTES: Do not lift to check maintain continuous pressure for a full 10 minutes.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:15
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: IF DEEP TEAR: If the wound is deep and pressure alone does not control it, gently pack clean cloth into the vaginal opening and maintain external pressure on top.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:16
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: TREAT FOR BLOOD LOSS: Encourage fluids if conscious.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:17
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: EVACUATE: Lacerations need suturing to fully stop bleeding and prevent infection.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:18
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Distinguish tear bleeding from uterine bleeding: press on the uterus.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:19
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If the uterus is firm but bleeding continues, the source is a tear, not the uterus.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:20
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Both can occur simultaneously.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:21
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Newborn Infection (Neonatal Sepsis) Source: WHO Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children; UNHCR Newborn Health in Humanitarian Settings.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:22
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Newborn infection (sepsis) is one of the leading causes of neonatal death worldwide.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:23
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: It develops in the first hours to days after birth, particularly after delivery in non-sterile conditions.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:24
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: It can kill within 2448 hours if untreated.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:25
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: SIGNS WATCH FOR THESE IN FIRST 3 DAYS [Page 9] Baby refuses to feed or feeds very weakly when previously feeding well Fever: baby feels hot to touch on the belly or back (OR is abnormally cold both are danger signs) Weak, high-pitched, or unusual cry or no cry at all Belly looks swollen or hard

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:0
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: 3 DAYS [Page 9] Baby refuses to feed or feeds very weakly when previously feeding well Fever: baby feels hot to touch on the belly or back (OR is abnormally cold both are danger signs) Weak, high-pitched, or unusual cry or no cry at all Belly looks swollen or hard Skin turns yellow (jaundice) in first 24 hours abnormal, not normal newborn jaundice Rapid breathing (more than 60 breaths per minute) or grunting sounds Baby is limp, floppy, not moving normally Redness, swelling, or discharge around the umbilical cord stump FIELD CARE 44.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:1
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: KEEP WARM: Skin-to-skin contact with the mother is the best way to maintain safe temperature.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:2
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Septic babies lose heat fast.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:3
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: BREASTFEED: Breast milk contains antibodies that fight infection.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:4
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Attempt breastfeeding every 12 hours.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:5
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If the baby is too weak to suck, try expressing milk and giving it by spoon or clean finger.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:6
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: KEEP THE CORD CLEAN: Do not apply anything to the cord stump except letting it air dry.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:7
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If the cord is infected (red, smelly, discharging pus), cover loosely with clean dry cloth.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:8
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: DO NOT GIVE HERBAL REMEDIES OR LOCAL TREATMENTS to a sick newborn.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:9
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: EVACUATE URGENTLY: Neonatal sepsis requires intravenous antibiotics.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:10
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: There is no effective field treatment.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:11
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: A baby that stops feeding is always a medical emergency.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:12
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Do not wait to see if it improves on its own.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:13
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Umbilical Cord Problems Source: WHO Basic Newborn Care Guidelines; MSF Neonatal Protocols.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:14
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Cord Bleeding After Cutting After the cord is cut and tied, the cut end should stop bleeding quickly.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:15
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If it continues to bleed, the tie was not tight enough.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:16
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: RE-TIE the cord tightly with clean string, cloth strip, or shoelace as close to the baby's belly as possible without crushing the skin.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:17
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If you have no tie: pinch the cord end between fingers and hold for 5 minutes.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:18
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: A small amount of oozing is normal.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:19
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Active dripping or flowing is not.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:20
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Cord Around the Baby's Neck During Birth (Nuchal Cord) [Page 10] Finding the umbilical cord wrapped around the baby's neck during delivery is common and usually manageable.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:21
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: FEEL for the cord around the neck as the baby's head delivers run one finger around the neck.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:22
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If the cord is LOOSE: gently slip it over the baby's head or over the baby's body as it delivers.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:23
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Do this calmly and without pulling.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:0
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: common and usually manageable.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:1
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: FEEL for the cord around the neck as the baby's head delivers run one finger around the neck.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:2
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If the cord is LOOSE: gently slip it over the baby's head or over the baby's body as it delivers.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:3
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Do this calmly and without pulling.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:4
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If the cord is TIGHT and cannot be slipped free: DO NOT FORCE IT.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:5
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Continue with the delivery.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:6
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Guide the baby's body out in the normal direction the cord will stretch.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:7
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Do not pull or cut the cord at this stage.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:8
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: After full delivery: manage cord bleeding as above.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:9
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Never cut a cord that is tightly around the neck before the baby is fully delivered this removes the baby's oxygen supply before it can breathe on its own.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:10
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Premature Baby (Born Too Early) Source: WHO Kangaroo Mother Care: A Practical Guide (2003); MSF Neonatal Care in Resource-Limited Settings.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:11
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: A baby born before 37 weeks of pregnancy is premature.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:12
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Premature babies are smaller, have thinner skin, and lose heat many times faster than full-term babies.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:13
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Hypothermia is the primary killer of premature infants in field conditions.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:14
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: RECOGNIZING A PREMATURE BABY Smaller and lighter than expected Thin, almost transparent or red skin Little body fat ribs may be visible Head appears proportionally larger Less active, weaker cry, weaker sucking reflex May have difficulty breathing rapid breathing, nostrils flaring, skin pulling in at ribs IMMEDIATE ACTIONS WARMTH IS SURVIVAL 56.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:15
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: DRY IMMEDIATELY: Dry the baby vigorously and discard the wet cloth.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:16
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Do not leave the baby on any wet surface even for a moment.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:17
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: SKIN-TO-SKIN WITHOUT INTERRUPTION: Place the baby directly on the mother's bare chest in an upright position between her breasts.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:18
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Cover both completely head included with warm dry cloth.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:19
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: This is called Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) and is the single most effective intervention available without equipment.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:20
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: KEEP SKIN-TO-SKIN CONTINUOUSLY: Unlike a full-term baby, a premature baby must remain in skin-to-skin contact at all times 24 hours a day until it is larger and stronger.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:21
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Even brief removal causes dangerous cooling.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:22
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: FEED FREQUENTLY: Attempt breastfeeding every 12 hours.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:23
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If the baby cannot latch due to weakness, express milk and give by clean spoon or dropper.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:24
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: A premature baby that is not fed will deteriorate rapidly.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:25
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: MONITOR BREATHING: Count breaths.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:26
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Normal for premature newborn is 4060 per minute.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:27
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Over 60 with visible effort

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:0
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Attempt breastfeeding every 12 hours.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:1
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If the baby cannot latch due to weakness, express milk and give by clean spoon or dropper.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:2
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: A premature baby that is not fed will deteriorate rapidly.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:3
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: MONITOR BREATHING: Count breaths.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:4
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Normal for premature newborn is 4060 per minute.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:5
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Over 60 with visible effort is a danger sign.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:6
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: EVACUATE: Premature babies under 34 weeks gestation require specialist care.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:7
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Begin evacuation while maintaining kangaroo care it can continue during transport.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:8
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Kangaroo Mother Care is endorsed by WHO as equal to incubator care in stable premature infants.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:9
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: It requires nothing except warmth and proximity.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:10
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Any adult (not just the mother) can provide it if the mother is unable.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:11
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Maternal Fever and Infection After Birth (Puerperal Sepsis) Source: WHO Managing Complications in Pregnancy and Childbirth (2017).

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:12
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Infection of the uterus or birth canal after delivery (puerperal sepsis) is a leading cause of maternal death.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:13
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: It typically appears 24 hours to several days after birth.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:14
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: SIGNS Fever (body feels hot, especially after the first 24 hours post-delivery) Foul-smelling discharge from the vagina Increasing belly pain and tenderness General weakness, chills, rapid pulse Mother appears increasingly unwell rather than recovering FIELD CARE 62.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:15
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Keep her hydrated encourage water and fluids constantly if she is not vomiting.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:16
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Keep her warm but do not overheat.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:17
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Continue breastfeeding infection does not pass to the baby through breast milk in most cases.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:18
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Do NOT apply anything inside the vagina.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:19
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: EVACUATE URGENTLY: Puerperal sepsis requires antibiotics.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:20
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Without treatment it progresses to septic shock and death within days.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:21
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Shrapnel & Shard Injuries Source: Tactical Combat Casualty Care (TCCC) Guidelines, Committee on TCCC (2023); International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) War Surgery, Volume 1.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:22
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Shrapnel injuries result from fragments metal, glass, bone, or debris entering the body at high velocity.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:23
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: A single explosion can cause dozens of entry wounds.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:24
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: The most immediately life- threatening are wounds that cause severe bleeding or penetrate the chest or abdomen.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:25
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Assess the Injury Do This First Zone Priority Head / Neck CRITICAL risk of airway loss, major vessel bleeding Chest (front or back) CRITICAL risk of collapsed lung, heart tamponade Abdomen / groin CRITICAL internal bleeding likely Arms and legs HIGH control bleeding first Small embedded fragments in skin LOW do not remove in the field 2B.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:26
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Controlling Life-Threatening Bleeding from Shrapnel IMMEDIATE ACTIONS 67.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:0
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Chest (front or back) CRITICAL risk of collapsed lung, heart tamponade Abdomen / groin CRITICAL internal bleeding likely Arms and legs HIGH control bleeding first Small embedded fragments in skin LOW do not remove in the field 2B.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:1
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Controlling Life-Threatening Bleeding from Shrapnel IMMEDIATE ACTIONS 67.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:2
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: EXPOSE: Cut away or remove clothing from around the wound to see it clearly.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:3
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: DIRECT PRESSURE: Press the cleanest material available (clothing, clean cloth) firmly and directly over the wound.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:4
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Use your palm or your fist for deep wounds.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:5
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: PACK THE WOUND: If the wound is deep or a hole (not a surface cut), push clean cloth INTO the wound with your finger.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:6
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: This is called wound packing.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:7
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: MAINTAIN PRESSURE: Hold firm pressure for a minimum of 10 minutes without lifting.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:8
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If blood soaks through, add more material on top do not remove the first layer.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:9
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: TOURNIQUET FOR LIMB WOUNDS: If bleeding is from an arm or leg and cannot be controlled with pressure, apply a tourniquet (see tourniquet instructions below).

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:10
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: DO NOT REMOVE EMBEDDED OBJECTS: If a large piece of shrapnel, glass, or metal is embedded in the body, do NOT pull it out.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:11
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: It may be plugging a vessel.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:12
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Stabilize it in place by padding around it.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:13
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Improvised Tourniquet Limbs Only A tourniquet stops blood flow to a limb.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:14
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Use it only when direct pressure fails and the wound is on an arm or leg.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:15
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: It will cause pain but saves lives.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:16
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Use a strip of cloth at least 4 cm (2 inches) wide a torn shirt sleeve, belt, or scarf.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:17
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Wrap it around the limb 58 cm (23 inches) ABOVE the wound (closer to the body, not below it).

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:18
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Tie a half-knot, place a stick or pen on the knot, tie another knot over the stick.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:19
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Twist the stick until bleeding stops.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:20
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: The person will feel severe pain this is expected.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:21
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Secure the stick so it cannot unwind.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:22
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Write the time applied on the person's forehead or arm with anything available.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:23
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Do NOT remove the tourniquet.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:24
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Only a medical professional should remove it.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:25
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: A tourniquet left on longer than 2 hours increases risk of limb loss.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:26
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Evacuation to medical care is urgent.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:0
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: the person's forehead or arm with anything available.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:1
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Do NOT remove the tourniquet.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:2
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Only a medical professional should remove it.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:3
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: A tourniquet left on longer than 2 hours increases risk of limb loss.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:4
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Evacuation to medical care is urgent.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:5
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Chest Wound from Shrapnel (Sucking Chest Wound) A wound that penetrates the chest wall allows air to enter the chest cavity, collapsing the lung.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:6
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: You may hear a sucking or hissing sound with each breath.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:7
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: SIGNS Wound in the chest that makes a sucking or bubbling sound when breathing Breathing becomes increasingly difficult and rapid Lips or fingernails turn blue Victim becomes agitated, then unresponsive IMMEDIATE ACTIONS 80.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:8
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: SEAL THE WOUND: Place the cleanest material available (plastic bag, plastic wrapper, tape) over the wound.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:9
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Tape 3 sides only leave one side open to act as a valve.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:10
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If no tape: hold the seal in place with your hand.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:11
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: SIT THEM UP: Help the person sit upright or lean slightly toward the injured side.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:12
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: This helps the good lung work better.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:13
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: MONITOR: If the person suddenly gets much worse (extreme breathing difficulty, veins in neck bulging, trachea shifting to one side), carefully lift the seal for 12 seconds to release trapped air, then re-seal.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:14
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: EVACUATE IMMEDIATELY: A chest wound requires surgical care.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:15
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: [Page 14] Do NOT seal ALL four sides of a chest wound.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:16
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: A fully sealed wound can trap air and create a tension pneumothorax which kills faster than the open wound.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:17
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Small Embedded Fragments Field Care Multiple small fragments embedded in skin (common in blast injuries) are not immediately life- threatening.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:18
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: In the field without sterile tools, removal attempts often cause more harm than the fragments themselves.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:19
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: DO NOT attempt to remove small embedded fragments without proper tools and lighting Rinse the area with clean water if available Cover loosely with any clean material to reduce infection risk Mark the locations with a pen if possible to assist later medical care Priority is always the life threats: bleeding, airway, breathing 2F.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:20
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Eye Penetration by Shrapnel or Shard Source: ICRC War Surgery Volume 1; Kuhn F.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:21
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: et al., Ocular Traumatology, Springer (2008).

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:22
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Eye injuries from fragments are extremely common in blast and explosion events.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:23
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Any penetrating object in the eye is a surgical emergency.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:24
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: The instinct to remove it is dangerous and must be suppressed.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:0
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: or Shard Source: ICRC War Surgery Volume 1; Kuhn F.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:1
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: et al., Ocular Traumatology, Springer (2008).

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:2
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Eye injuries from fragments are extremely common in blast and explosion events.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:3
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Any penetrating object in the eye is a surgical emergency.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:4
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: The instinct to remove it is dangerous and must be suppressed.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:5
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: SIGNS Visible object (fragment, glass, metal) in or on the eye Severe eye pain, or complete absence of pain (which may indicate deep penetration) Sudden loss of vision or blurred vision in the affected eye Eye appears deformed, sunken, or fluid leaking from the eye Blood in the white part of the eye or visible beneath the surface IMMEDIATE ACTIONS 84.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:6
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: DO NOT REMOVE THE OBJECT: Even a small fragment may be holding eye fluid in place.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:7
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Removal causes immediate loss of eye contents and permanent blindness.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:8
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: DO NOT RUB OR PRESS THE EYE: Any pressure on a penetrated eye can force internal contents out.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:9
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: COVER BOTH EYES: This is critical.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:10
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: The eyes move together if only the injured eye is covered, movement of the uncovered eye will cause the injured eye to move too, [Page 15] worsening damage.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:11
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Cover both eyes with a clean cloth or cup shape (do not press on the eye itself let the covering arch over it without touching).

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:12
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: KEEP THE PERSON STILL: Ask them not to move their head.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:13
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Lay them flat if possible.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:14
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: KEEP THEM CALM: Fear and movement worsen outcome.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:15
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: EVACUATE URGENTLY: Eye penetration requires surgical care within hours to preserve vision.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:16
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Covering BOTH eyes is not optional it is medically necessary.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:17
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Explain this clearly to the person.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:18
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Moving one eye moves both.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:19
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Neck Injuries from Shrapnel Source: TCCC Guidelines; ATLS 10th Edition Neck Trauma.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:20
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: The neck contains the largest blood vessels in the body (carotid arteries and jugular veins), the airway (trachea), and the spinal cord.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:21
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: A shrapnel wound to the neck can kill in under 2 minutes from bleeding alone.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:22
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: SIGNS OF DANGEROUS NECK INJURY Active bleeding from the neck even moderate bleeding here is life-threatening Expanding swelling or bruising in the neck (blood pooling under skin) Hoarse voice, difficulty speaking, or stridor (high-pitched breathing sound) Difficulty swallowing or speaking after a neck wound Bubbling or hissing from a neck wound (trachea/airway injury) IMMEDIATE ACTIONS 90.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:23
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: DIRECT PRESSURE ONLY: Press clean cloth firmly over the bleeding area.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:24
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11

s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: NEVER USE A TOURNIQUET ON THE NECK: A tourniquet around the neck stops blood flow to the brain and kills instantly.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12:4
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: DO NOT PACK AGGRESSIVELY: Deep packing of neck wounds risks compressing the airway or causing further vessel damage.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12:5

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12:6
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12:7
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If breathing worsens, open the airway (head tilt/chin lift, see Section 5B) and be ready to give rescue breaths.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12:8
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: KEEP HEAD STILL: Avoid unnecessary movement of the neck.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12:9
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If spinal injury is possible (blast threw the person), keep the head and neck aligned.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12:10
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: EVACUATE IMMEDIATELY: Neck injuries are among the highest-priority evacuations.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12:11
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: [Page 16] A neck wound that appears small can still be cutting a major vessel internally.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12:12
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Do not be reassured by a small external wound.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12:13
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Treat all neck wounds as life- threatening.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12:15
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Shrapnel penetrating the abdomen causes the same internal injuries as a gunshot wound to the abdomen.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12:16
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: There is no field treatment for internal abdominal bleeding only stabilization and evacuation.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12:17
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: SIGNS Entry wound on the abdomen, side, or lower back Belly becomes progressively hard, rigid, and painful Signs of shock: pale, sweating, rapid weak pulse, confusion Visible bowel or tissue protruding from wound FIELD CARE 96.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12:18
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: DO NOT pack the abdominal wound deeply with cloth this worsens internal injury.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12:19
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: DO NOT push any protruding tissue back inside.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12:20
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: COVER the wound loosely with the cleanest damp material available.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12:21
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If an object is embedded: stabilize it with padding on all sides do not remove.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12:22
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: NOTHING BY MOUTH: No water, no food surgery will be needed.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12:23
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: LAY FLAT: Allow knees to bend if more comfortable.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12:24
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: TREAT FOR SHOCK: Keep warm, elevate legs gently.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12:25
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: EVACUATE URGENTLY: Internal abdominal injuries are universally fatal without surgery.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12:26
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Multiple Small Wounds Triage Priority Source: TCCC Tactical Field Care Guidelines; NATO Mass Casualty Management.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12:27
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_12
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: In blast events, a single person may have 20 or more separate fragment wounds.

t: EVACUATE URGENTLY: Internal abdominal injuries are universally fatal without surgery.

c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13

c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: In blast events, a single person may have 20 or more separate fragment wounds.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13:4
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: The natural instinct is to address the most visible wound.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13:5
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: The most visible wound is often not the most dangerous one.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13:6
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: [Page 17] THE CORRECT APPROACH 104.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13:7
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: EXPOSE THE WHOLE BODY: Before treating any single wound, quickly cut or remove clothing to view the entire body surface.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13:8
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: This takes 3060 seconds and saves lives.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13:9
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: FIND THE BIGGEST BLEED FIRST: Look for the wound with the fastest active bleeding.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13:10
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: A wound soaking cloth in seconds outranks one that is oozing slowly.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13:11
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: USE THE ZONE TABLE (Section 2A): Identify which zone the worst wound is in and prioritize accordingly.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13:12
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: TREAT LIFE THREATS IN ORDER: Massive bleeding airway breathing all other wounds.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13:13
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: MARK TREATED WOUNDS: Use pen, chalk, or mud to mark wounds that have been dressed so nothing is missed.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13:14
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Small wounds in critical zones (neck, chest, abdomen) are more dangerous than large wounds on the arms and legs.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13:15
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Infection Risk from Shrapnel Wounds Source: ICRC War Surgery; WHO Wound Management Guidelines.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13:16
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Shrapnel carries dirt, clothing fibers, and bacteria deep into tissue.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13:17
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: All shrapnel wounds are considered contaminated.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13:18
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Infection typically develops 2472 hours after injury and can become life-threatening within days without antibiotics.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13:19
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: SIGNS OF WOUND INFECTION (appearing 2472 hours later) Increasing redness spreading from the wound edges Increasing pain and swelling around the wound Warmth around the wound Pus or cloudy discharge from the wound Red streaks extending from the wound toward the body (sign of spreading infection emergency) Fever, chills, increasing weakness FIELD PREVENTION AND CARE 109.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13:20
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: RINSE ALL WOUNDS WITH CLEAN WATER immediately after injury.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13:21
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Use as much as available irrigation reduces infection risk more than any other field measure.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13:22
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: COVER WITH CLEAN DRY MATERIAL: All wounds should be covered to keep them clean.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13:23
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: DO NOT CLOSE DIRTY WOUNDS: Do not tie, tape, or suture shrapnel wounds closed in the field.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13:24
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Trapping contamination inside causes gangrene.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13:25
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: CHANGE DRESSINGS DAILY if possible, using the cleanest available material each time.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13:26
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: IF INFECTION DEVELOPS: Evacuate.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13:27
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_13
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Field treatment cannot adequately treat deep wound infection.

c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14:5
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14

t: RED STREAKS FROM A WOUND: This is a medical emergency.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14:6
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Septicemia (blood poisoning) can develop within hours.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14:7
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Do not close shrapnel wounds.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14:8
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Closed contaminated wounds can cause fatal gas gangrene.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14:9
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Fractures Caused by Shrapnel Impact Source: PHTLS 9th Edition; NATO Emergency War Surgery.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14:10
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: High-velocity fragments carry enough energy to shatter bone even when they do not penetrate deeply.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14:11
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: An open fracture (bone visible or wound near broken bone) is both an orthopedic and infection emergency.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14:12
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: SIGNS OF FRACTURE Deformity limb looks bent or out of position Inability or refusal to move the limb Severe local pain and swelling Grinding or grating sensation Bone visible through the wound (open fracture highest infection risk) FIELD CARE 115.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14:13
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: DO NOT STRAIGHTEN THE LIMB: Immobilize it in the position you find it.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14:14
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Forced straightening causes additional vessel and nerve damage.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14:15
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: SPLINT IN PLACE: Use any rigid material (stick, board, rolled clothing) alongside the limb and tie above and below the fracture not over it.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14:16
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: The splint should extend beyond the joints above and below the fracture.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14:17
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: CHECK CIRCULATION: After splinting, check that fingers or toes below the fracture are still warm and can be felt.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14:18
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If they are cold, pale, or numb, the splint may be too tight loosen slightly.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14:19
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: COVER OPEN FRACTURES: If bone is visible, cover loosely with the cleanest damp cloth.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14:20
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Treat as a wound with high infection risk.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14:21
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: ELEVATE THE LIMB: If possible, rest the limb elevated above heart level to reduce swelling.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14:22
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: EVACUATE: Open fractures require surgical cleaning within hours to prevent bone infection (osteomyelitis).

s: field_emergency_guide_v2

c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14

t: Most deaths from GSW are due to bleeding.

c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_14

t: Step Action M Massive Hemorrhage Stop all life-threatening bleeding first, before anything else A Airway Ensure the person can breathe; open and clear the airway R Respiration Check and treat chest injuries C Circulation Treat shock; keep them warm and horizontal H Hypothermia Prevent heat loss; cover immediately 3B.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15:6
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15:7
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: DIRECT PRESSURE: Press hard on the wound with the cleanest material available.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15:8
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Press as hard as you physically can.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15:9
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: WOUND PACKING: For bullet holes push clean cloth deep into the wound with your fingers.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15:10
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: TOURNIQUET: For arm or leg wounds with uncontrollable bleeding, apply improvised tourniquet (see Section 2C).

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15:11
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Apply HIGH and TIGHT as close to the armpit or groin as possible.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15:12
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: JUNCTIONAL WOUNDS (groin, armpit, neck): These areas cannot be tourniqueted.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15:13
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Apply direct pressure with your full body weight.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15:14
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Junctional wounds (where the limb meets the body groin, armpit) are extremely dangerous and cannot have a tourniquet applied.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15:15
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Constant manual pressure is the only field option.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15:16
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Airway Ensure They Can Breathe 125.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15:17
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If conscious and talking: their airway is open.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15:18
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If unconscious: tilt the head back gently and lift the chin up.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15:19
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Sweep the mouth with a finger: remove blood, vomit, teeth, or debris.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15:20
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Turn them on their side (recovery position) if they are breathing but unconscious, to prevent choking on blood or vomit.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15:21
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Head Gunshot Wound Head wounds bleed profusely even when not life-threatening.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15:22
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Assess consciousness immediately.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15:23
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Apply gentle direct pressure to scalp wounds do NOT press hard on skull wounds where the bone may be damaged If unconscious but breathing: recovery position (on side), clear airway Do NOT remove any object embedded in the skull Do NOT give anything to eat or drink Speak calmly even if they appear unconscious hearing may remain Protect from heat and cold Evacuate immediately any loss of consciousness after head GSW requires urgent care 3E.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15:24
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_15
