t: Do NOT remove any object embedded in the skull Do NOT give anything to eat or drink Speak calmly even if they appear unconscious hearing may remain Protect from heat and cold Evacuate immediately any loss of consciousness after head GSW requires urgent care 3E.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16:1
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Abdominal Gunshot Wound Abdominal GSW causes internal bleeding that cannot be controlled in the field.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16:2
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: The only treatment is surgery.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16:3
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: SIGNS OF ABDOMINAL GSW Entry wound on abdomen, back, or flank Belly becomes rigid and painful over time Intestines or tissue visible through the wound Signs of shock: pale, sweating, rapid weak pulse, confusion FIELD CARE 129.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16:4
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: DO NOT push protruding organs back in.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16:5
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Cover them with the cleanest damp cloth available.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16:6
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: DO NOT remove any object from the abdomen.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16:7
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Apply a large loose dressing over the wound do not pack tightly.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16:8
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If they are more comfortable with knees bent, allow it.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16:9
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Give nothing by mouth no water, no food.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16:10
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: EVACUATE URGENTLY internal abdominal bleeding is fatal without surgery.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16:11
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: This is a transport priority.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16:12
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Treating Shock Shock is the body's response to losing too much blood.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16:13
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: It is a medical emergency.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16:14
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Sign of Shock Severity Anxious, slightly pale, thirsty Early act now Pale, sweating, confused, rapid pulse Moderate urgent Unresponsive, barely breathing, no pulse at Severe critical wrist Field Treatment for Shock 136.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16:15
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Raise legs 30 cm if no spinal injury suspected.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16:16
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Keep them warm cover with everything available.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16:17
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If conscious and not abdominal GSW: small sips of water or oral rehydration salts.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16:18
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Reassess pulse every 5 minutes.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16:19
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Blast Injuries / Explosion Source: TCCC Guidelines; NATO Emergency War Surgery (4th Edition); Blast Injury Research Program, US Army Medical Research.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16:20
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Explosions cause four distinct types of injury that can all occur in the same person simultaneously.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16:21
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: This is what makes blast injury more complex than a single wound.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16:22
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Blast Injury Type What It Means Primary pressure wave Invisible wave of pressure damages lungs, eardrums, bowel, and sinuses Secondary fragments Shrapnel and debris cause penetrating wounds (see Section 2) Tertiary thrown Person is thrown through the air, causing fractures and crush injuries Quaternary burns/crush Burns, building collapse, toxic gas inhalation 4A.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16:23
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_16
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Immediate Scene Actions Do NOT rush

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17:0
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: wave Invisible wave of pressure damages lungs, eardrums, bowel, and sinuses Secondary fragments Shrapnel and debris cause penetrating wounds (see Section 2) Tertiary thrown Person is thrown through the air, causing fractures and crush injuries Quaternary burns/crush Burns, building collapse, toxic gas inhalation 4A.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17:1
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Immediate Scene Actions Do NOT rush to victims immediately after an explosion.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17:2
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Secondary devices (second bombs placed to target rescuers) are common in conflict zones.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17:3
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Wait 60 seconds and scan the area before approaching.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17:4
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: ENSURE SCENE IS SAFE: Scan for fire, structural collapse risk, gas leaks (smell), and secondary threats.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17:5
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: TRIAGE IF MULTIPLE VICTIMS: Quickly walk through and identify who is walking (minor), who is on the ground but breathing (urgent), who is not moving and not breathing (critical/expectant).

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17:6
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: CALL FOR HELP: Send someone to get any available medical assistance while you begin care.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17:7
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Primary Blast Lung Injury The pressure wave can rupture the tiny air sacs in the lungs without any external wound.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17:8
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: This is called blast lung and may not be obvious immediately it can worsen over hours.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17:9
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: SIGNS MAY APPEAR WITHIN MINUTES TO HOURS AFTER BLAST Coughing up blood or pink foamy sputum Shortness of breath that worsens over time [Page 24] Chest pain, especially when breathing deeply The person was close to the blast even if they appear fine Low oxygen: lips, fingernails, or gums turn blue FIELD CARE 145.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17:10
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Sit the person upright do not lay flat if they have breathing difficulty 146.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17:11
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Keep them calm and still exertion worsens blast lung 147.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17:12
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Monitor breathing closely.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17:13
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Count breaths per minute (normal is 1220) 148.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17:14
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If they have both blast lung AND a chest wound: treat the chest wound first (see 2D) 149.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17:15
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Evacuate: blast lung can become fatal within hours 4C.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17:16
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Blast Ear Injury (Ruptured Eardrum) The eardrum ruptures under blast pressure.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17:17
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: This is extremely common and usually not life- threatening, but the person may be disoriented.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17:18
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Signs: ringing in ears, hearing loss, pain, blood from ear canal, dizziness Cover the ear loosely with clean cloth do not insert anything into the ear canal Do NOT irrigate or flush the ear A person with blast ear injury may not be able to follow verbal instructions use hand signals and touch Most ruptures heal on their own but require medical assessment to rule out deeper injury 4D.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17:19
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_17
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Traumatic Amputation from Blast High-order blasts can cause partial or complete

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18:0
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: or flush the ear A person with blast ear injury may not be able to follow verbal instructions use hand signals and touch Most ruptures heal on their own but require medical assessment to rule out deeper injury 4D.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18:1
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Traumatic Amputation from Blast High-order blasts can cause partial or complete traumatic amputation of limbs.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18:2
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: TOURNIQUET IMMEDIATELY: Apply as high on the limb as possible before doing anything else.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18:3
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: A traumatic amputation will bleed fatally within minutes.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18:4
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: PACK THE STUMP: If the tourniquet does not fully control bleeding, pack clean cloth tightly into the wound and press hard.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18:5
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: DO NOT try to reattach or preserve the amputated part in field conditions without ice focus entirely on keeping the person alive.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18:6
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: TREAT FOR SHOCK: Lay flat, keep warm, elevate legs.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18:7
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Building Collapse / Crush Injury If a person has been trapped under rubble or a heavy object for more than 15 minutes, releasing them can trigger a dangerous reaction called crush syndrome, where toxins released from damaged muscle can cause heart failure.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18:8
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If a person has been trapped for more than 15 minutes under heavy weight, DO NOT move them without medical guidance if any is available.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18:9
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Releasing the pressure too quickly without IV fluids can cause sudden cardiac arrest.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18:10
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If you MUST move them: move quickly and be prepared for sudden collapse Lay them flat immediately after extraction Encourage drinking large amounts of water if conscious Look for swollen, hard, dark limbs sign of crush injury Evacuate urgently crush syndrome requires hospital treatment 4F.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18:11
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Burns from Blast Source: WHO Burns Management; ICRC War Surgery.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18:12
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Burn Severity What it looks like Minor (1st degree) Red, painful skin, like a sunburn.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18:13
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Moderate (2nd degree) Blisters, very painful, wet-looking skin Severe (3rd degree) White, brown, or black leathery skin.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18:14
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Field Treatment for Burns 155.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18:15
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: COOL THE BURN: Pour cool (not ice cold) water over the burn for 1020 minutes.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18:16
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: This is the only burn first aid that changes outcomes.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18:17
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: COVER: After cooling, cover loosely with clean dry material.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18:18
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: DO NOT: burst blisters, apply toothpaste, oil, butter, or any home remedy these cause infection and make burns worse.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18:19
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: DO NOT remove clothing stuck to a burn cut around it.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18:20
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_18
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: FACE BURNS: If eyebrows are singed and the person has a

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19:0
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: DO NOT: burst blisters, apply toothpaste, oil, butter, or any home remedy these cause infection and make burns worse.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19:1
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: DO NOT remove clothing stuck to a burn cut around it.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19:2
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: FACE BURNS: If eyebrows are singed and the person has a hoarse voice or difficulty swallowing, the airway may be burned internally.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19:3
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: This is a critical emergency requiring immediate evacuation.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19:4
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: TREAT FOR SHOCK: Severe burns cause massive fluid loss and shock.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19:5
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Airway & Breathing Emergencies Source: TCCC Guidelines; WHO Basic Emergency Care (BEC); American Heart Association CPR Guidelines (2020); Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) 10th Edition.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19:6
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Airway and breathing emergencies are the most rapidly fatal conditions.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19:7
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Without oxygen, brain damage begins in 4 minutes and death follows within 10.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19:8
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: These must be treated before any other injury except massive bleeding.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19:9
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Assess Breathing Do This First for Every Patient 161.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19:10
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: LOOK: Is the chest rising and falling?

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19:11
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: LISTEN: Put your ear near the mouth and nose.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19:12
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Can you hear breath sounds?

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19:13
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: FEEL: Can you feel air against your cheek?

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19:14
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Finding Action Breathing normally Go to next priority bleeding, wounds Breathing noisily (gurgling, snoring) Clear airway see 5B Breathing very fast (>30 per min) Suspect chest injury see Section 2D or 4B Not breathing Begin rescue breaths immediately see 5C Not breathing, no pulse Begin CPR see 5D 5B.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19:15
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Opening and Clearing the Airway If the person is unconscious: 164.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19:16
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: HEAD TILT-CHIN LIFT: Place one hand on the forehead, two fingers under the chin.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19:17
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Tilt head back and lift chin.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19:18
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: This straightens the airway.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19:19
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If spinal injury is suspected (fall, blast threw them, neck pain mentioned): use JAW THRUST instead place fingers behind the jaw angle and push the jaw forward without tilting the head.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19:20
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: SWEEP THE MOUTH: Use your finger to clear blood, vomit, broken teeth, or debris from the mouth.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19:21
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Only sweep what you can see.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19:22
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: RECOVERY POSITION: If breathing has returned turn them on their side so vomit drains out and the tongue cannot block the airway.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19:23
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Airway Blocked by a Solid Object Conscious Adult 168.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19:24
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Ask: 'Are you choking?' If they cannot speak or cough, they need help.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19:25
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: BACK BLOWS: Give 5 firm blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19:26
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_19
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: ABDOMINAL THRUSTS (Heimlich): Stand behind them, place one fist above the

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20:0
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: a Solid Object Conscious Adult 168.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20:1
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Ask: 'Are you choking?' If they cannot speak or cough, they need help.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20:2
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: BACK BLOWS: Give 5 firm blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20:3
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: ABDOMINAL THRUSTS (Heimlich): Stand behind them, place one fist above the navel below the breastbone, cover with other hand, and give 5 sharp upward thrusts.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20:4
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until the object is expelled or the person becomes unconscious.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20:5
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If unconscious: begin CPR each time you open the airway to give a breath, look in the mouth for the object.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20:6
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: For pregnant women or people who are very obese: use chest thrusts (same position but hands on the center of the chest) instead of abdominal thrusts.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20:7
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Rescue Breathing Person Not Breathing, Has Pulse 173.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20:8
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Tilt head back, lift chin.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20:9
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Take a normal breath, seal your lips completely around their mouth.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20:10
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Breathe in gently just enough to see the chest rise (about 1 second).

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20:11
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Give 1 breath every 56 seconds (about 1012 breaths per minute).

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20:12
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Check for pulse every 2 minutes.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20:13
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If you cannot or will not do mouth-to-mouth: covering the face with a thin cloth allows breath to pass through while reducing direct contact.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20:14
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: CPR No Breathing and No Pulse CPR (Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation) keeps blood and oxygen circulating when the heart has stopped.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20:15
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Even imperfect CPR dramatically improves survival.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20:16
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: CPR STEPS ADULTS AND CHILDREN OVER 8 YEARS 179.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20:17
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: POSITION: Lay the person on their back on a firm surface.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20:18
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: HEEL OF HAND: Place the heel of one hand on the center of the chest (lower half of the breastbone).

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20:19
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Place the other hand on top and interlock fingers.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20:20
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: COMPRESS: Push straight down firmly and fast at least 56 cm (2 inches).

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20:21
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Let the chest fully rebound after each compression.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20:22
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Do not lean on the chest between compressions.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20:23
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: RATE: 100120 compressions per minute.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20:24
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: This is faster than one per second think of the rhythm of a fast song beat.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20:25
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: RATIO: Give 30 compressions, then 2 rescue breaths.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20:26
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If you cannot or will not give rescue breaths: give continuous chest compressions only at 100120 per minute without stopping.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20:27
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_20
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Continue until: the person wakes up, starts breathing, medical

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21:0
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: rhythm of a fast song beat.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21:1
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: RATIO: Give 30 compressions, then 2 rescue breaths.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21:2
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If you cannot or will not give rescue breaths: give continuous chest compressions only at 100120 per minute without stopping.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21:3
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Continue until: the person wakes up, starts breathing, medical help arrives, or you are physically unable to continue.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21:4
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: CPR for Infants (Under 1 Year) Use 2 fingers (middle and ring finger) on the center of the chest, just below the nipple line Compress about 4 cm (1.5 inches) 30 compressions to 2 gentle puffs (cover mouth AND nose together) 100120 compressions per minute CPR for Children (18 Years) Use the heel of one hand only Compress 5 cm (2 inches) 30 compressions to 2 rescue breaths CPR on a person who still has a heartbeat can cause heart problems.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21:5
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Only begin CPR if you are certain there is no pulse.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21:6
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Choking on Blood Trauma Airway In trauma, the airway is often blocked by blood rather than a foreign object.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21:7
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: This requires different management.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21:8
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: DO NOT do abdominal thrusts there is no solid object to dislodge.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21:9
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: ROLL ON SIDE: Turn the person onto their side so blood drains out of the mouth by gravity.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21:10
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: CLEAR WITH FINGER: If a blood clot is visible in the mouth, sweep it out with your finger.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21:11
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: SUCTION: If a suction device is available, use it.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21:12
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: If a neck or jaw wound is causing airway obstruction and the person is rapidly deteriorating, push the jaw forward and hold it there this lifts the tongue off the airway.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21:13
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Tension Pneumothorax Air Trapped in Chest This is one of the most rapidly fatal conditions after trauma.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21:14
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: It occurs when air builds up inside the chest cavity (from a lung wound or blast) and compresses the heart and remaining lung.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21:15
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: SIGNS THE PERSON IS DETERIORATING DESPITE TREATMENT [Page 29] Breathing becomes extremely difficult and rapid Neck veins bulge visibly The trachea (windpipe) shifts away from center of the neck Blood pressure collapses person becomes unresponsive This occurs after a chest wound has been sealed FIELD ACTION 191.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21:16
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: RELEASE THE SEAL: If a chest wound has been sealed (see 2D), lift the seal for 23 seconds to allow trapped air to escape.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21:17
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_21
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: POSITION: Sit upright if possible.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_22:0
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_22
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: person becomes unresponsive This occurs after a chest wound has been sealed FIELD ACTION 191.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_22:1
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_22
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: RELEASE THE SEAL: If a chest wound has been sealed (see 2D), lift the seal for 23 seconds to allow trapped air to escape.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_22:2
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_22
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: POSITION: Sit upright if possible.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_22:3
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_22
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: EVACUATE: This requires needle decompression (a medical procedure).

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_22:4
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_22
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: There is no improvised treatment.

i: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_22:5
c: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_22
s: field_emergency_guide_v2
t: Rapid evacuation is the only field option.

t: Every section uses the same structure: Section What It Tells You Overview What the condition is and why it is dangerous Signs & Symptoms How to recognise the condition Immediate Actions What to do first step by step, in order Ongoing Care What to keep doing until EMS arrives What NOT to Do Common mistakes that make things worse When to Call EMS/Move Explicit criteria for professional care THE UNIVERSAL FIRST CHECK DO THIS FOR EVERY H EMERGENCY Perform these 5 steps before treating any specific condition.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0:11
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: [Page 2] ENSURE SCENE SAFETY 1 Do not approach until the environment is safe.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0:12
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Check for traffic, fire, unstable structures, electrical hazards, or ongoing threats.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0:13
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Your safety comes first an injured responder helps no one.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0:14
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: CHECK RESPONSIVENESS 2 Shout the person's name and tap their shoulders firmly.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0:15
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: If no response, they are unresponsive.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0:16
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Shout for help immediately.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0:17
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: CALL EMS NOW 3 Call 911 (or your local emergency number) immediately or direct a specific bystander: 'YOU call 911 and come back to tell me.' Do not assume someone else has called.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0:18
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: CHECK BREATHING 4 Tilt the head back and look for chest rise for no more than 10 seconds.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0:19
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Normal breathing proceed to step 5.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0:21
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: CONTROL SEVERE BLEEDING 5 Look rapidly for blood soaking through clothing.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0:22
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Press hard with the cleanest material available.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0:23
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Then proceed to the specific condition section.

s: First_Aid_Guide

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:7
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: [Page 3] 1 CHOKING ADULT & INFANT Choking occurs when a foreign object food, a small toy, or fluid partially or completely blocks the airway.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:8
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: A complete blockage stops all air exchange and causes unconsciousness within minutes.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:9
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Immediate action prevents brain damage and death.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:10
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Choking Conscious Adult or Child (Over 1 Year) Signs & Symptoms (cid:127) Sudden inability to speak, cry, or make sound (cid:127) Clutching the throat with one or both hands (universal choking sign) (cid:127) Weak, ineffective, or absent cough (cid:127) High-pitched wheezing or no breathing sounds at all (cid:127) Face turns red, then blue (cyanosis) sign of severe hypoxia (cid:127) Panic, wide eyes, frantic gestures Immediate Actions 1.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:11
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: ASK: 'Are you choking?' If the person can speak or cough forcefully encourage them to keep coughing.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:12
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: IF THEY CANNOT SPEAK OR COUGH: Stand behind them.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:13
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Lean them slightly forward.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:14
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: BACK BLOWS: Give 5 firm blows between the shoulder blades using the heel of your hand.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:15
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Each blow should be a separate, distinct strike.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:16
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: ABDOMINAL THRUSTS (HEIMLICH): Place one fist above the navel and below the breastbone.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:17
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Grip your fist with your other hand.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:18
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Give 5 sharp inward-and-upward thrusts.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:19
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: ALTERNATE: Repeat 5 back blows, then 5 abdominal thrusts until the object is expelled, the person can breathe and cough, or they lose consciousness.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:20
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: IF UNCONSCIOUS: Lower them carefully to the ground.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:21

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2:10

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:7
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:8

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:9
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: CHECK BREATHING: Look for chest rise for no more than 10 seconds.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:10
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Gasping is NOT normal breathing.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:11
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
s: First_Aid_Guide

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:12
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: HAND PLACEMENT: Heel of one hand on the center of the chest (lower half of the breastbone).

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:13
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Second hand on top, fingers interlaced.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:14
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: COMPRESS: Push straight down at least 56 cm (22.4 inches).

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:15
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Allow full chest recoil between compressions.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:16
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: RATE: 100120 compressions per minute.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:17
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Count aloud: '1 and 2 and 3...' Think of a fast song beat.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:18
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: RESCUE BREATHS (if trained and willing): After 30 compressions tilt head back, lift chin, pinch nose, give 1 breath over 1 second just until chest rises.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:19
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Give 2 breaths, then resume compressions.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:20
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
s: First_Aid_Guide

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:21
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: This is effective and recommended.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:22
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
s: First_Aid_Guide

s: First_Aid_Guide

s: First_Aid_Guide

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:18

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:21

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:22

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5:11

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5:12

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5:13

t: Remove burning or smoldering clothing unless it is stuck to the skin, in which case cut around it, never pull.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:12
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: COOL THE BURN: Run cool (not cold, not icy) water over the burn for a full 1020 minutes.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:13
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Start within 3 hours of injury.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:14
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: This is the single most important intervention.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:15
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: REMOVE: Gently remove rings, watches, or tight clothing near the burn before swelling begins.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:16
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Do not remove if stuck to skin.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:17
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: COVER LOOSELY: After cooling, cover with a clean non-fluffy material cling film (plastic wrap) is ideal.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:18
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: A clean plastic bag works for hands.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:19
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: DO NOT BURST BLISTERS: Blisters are a natural protective layer.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:20
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Intact blisters reduce infection risk significantly.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:21
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: TREAT FOR SHOCK: Large or deep burns cause massive fluid loss.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:22
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Lay flat, keep warm if shivering, monitor for shock signs.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:23
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Chemical Burns Immediate Actions 1.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:24
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: PROTECT YOURSELF: Put on gloves or use a plastic bag before handling the patient or their clothing.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:25
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Chemical burns can burn through your skin too.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:26
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: REMOVE CLOTHING: Remove all contaminated clothing, shoes, and jewellery carefully.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:27
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Do not allow chemical contact with unaffected skin.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:28
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: FLUSH CONTINUOUSLY: Rinse the affected area with large amounts of cool running water for at least 20 minutes for acids, and 60 minutes or more for alkalis (bleach, lime, cement).

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:29
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: DO NOT NEUTRALISE: Do not apply baking soda to acid burns or vinegar to alkali burns.

t: DO NOT NEUTRALISE: Do not apply baking soda to acid burns or vinegar to alkali burns.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:2
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Neutralisation reactions generate heat and worsen injury.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:3
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: COVER: After flushing, cover loosely with clean dry material.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:4
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: CALL POISON CONTROL: In addition to EMS, call poison control if the chemical is known they can advise on specific antidotes or extended flushing times.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:5
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Face or Inhalation Burns Critical Signs n AIRWAY BURN CRITICAL EMERGENCY Singed eyebrows or nasal hair, hoarse voice, difficulty swallowing, or soot around the mouth/nose indicate a possible internal airway burn.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:6
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: The airway can swell shut within minutes to hours.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:7
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Do NOT wait for breathing difficulty to worsen.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:8
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Ongoing Care Keep the burned area elevated if possible.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:9
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Keep the person warm burned skin loses heat rapidly.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:10
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Offer small sips of water if conscious and no airway injury is suspected.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:11
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Do not remove the covering or re-expose the burn.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:12
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: n WHAT NOT TO DO Do NOT apply butter, oil, toothpaste, egg white, or any home remedy all cause infection and seal in heat.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:13
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Do NOT use ice or ice-cold water causes vasoconstriction and extends tissue damage.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:14
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Do NOT remove clothing that is stuck to burned skin cut around it.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:15
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Do NOT use fluffy cotton wool or adhesive bandages directly on burns.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:16:0
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: When to Call EMS (cid:127) Burns larger than the palm of the person's hand (approximately 1% body surface area) (cid:127) Burns on the face, hands, feet, genitals, or over a major joint (cid:127) Any 3rd degree burn, or suspected deep burn (cid:127) Any chemical burn to the eyes (cid:127) Suspected inhalation burn or airway involvement (cid:127) Burns in children under 5 or adults over 60 (cid:127) Burn caused by electricity always requires hospital evaluation even if minor-looking [Page 10] 5 SEVERE BLEEDING & DEEP CUTS Severe, uncontrolled bleeding is one of the most preventable causes of death.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:17
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: An adult can lose a fatal amount of blood in as little as 23 minutes from a major vessel injury.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:18
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Direct, firm, uninterrupted pressure is the primary life-saving action.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:19
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Improvised tourniquets on limbs are effective and appropriate when direct pressure fails.

c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
s: First_Aid_Guide

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:2

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:3
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Signs & Symptoms (cid:127) Blood soaking rapidly through clothing a soaked cloth in under 1 minute is severe (cid:127) Blood spurting with each heartbeat (arterial bleeding the most dangerous type) (cid:127) Signs of shock: pale skin, cold clammy sweat, rapid weak pulse, confusion, thirst (cid:127) Large wound with visible deep tissue, muscle, or bone Immediate Actions 1.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:4
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: PROTECT YOURSELF: Put on disposable gloves from your first aid kit if immediately available.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:5
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: EXPOSE THE WOUND: Cut or remove clothing around the wound to see it clearly and control it effectively.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:6
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: APPLY DIRECT PRESSURE: Place the cleanest available material (sterile gauze pad, clean cloth) directly over the wound.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:7
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Press as hard as you can with your palm or both hands.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:8
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: PACK DEEP WOUNDS: If the wound is a deep hole or cavity push clean gauze or cloth firmly into the wound with your fingers.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:9
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: This is called wound packing.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:10
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: HOLD PRESSURE: Maintain continuous firm pressure for a minimum of 10 full minutes without lifting to check.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:11
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: If blood soaks through add more material on top.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:12
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Do NOT remove the first layer.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:13
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: TOURNIQUET FOR LIMB WOUNDS: If bleeding from an arm or leg cannot be controlled with pressure after 23 minutes apply a tourniquet (see below).

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:14
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: ELEVATE: If the wound is on a limb and no fracture is suspected raise it above the level of the heart to slow blood flow.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:15
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: KEEP THEM CALM AND WARM: Fear increases heart rate and blood loss.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:16
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Improvised Tourniquet Limbs Only Use when direct pressure fails on an arm or leg wound.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:17
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Apply without hesitation when needed.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:18
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: MATERIAL: Use a strip of cloth at least 4 cm (2 inches) wide a torn shirt sleeve, belt, or scarf.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:19
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Never use wire, rope, or narrow cord they cut tissue.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:20
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: PLACEMENT: Wrap 58 cm (23 inches) ABOVE the wound (toward the body, not below).

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:21
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: TIGHTEN: Tie a half-knot, place a stick or pen on the knot, tie a second knot over it.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:0
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Never use wire, rope, or narrow cord they cut tissue.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:1
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: PLACEMENT: Wrap 58 cm (23 inches) ABOVE the wound (toward the body, not below).

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:2
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: TIGHTEN: Tie a half-knot, place a stick or pen on the knot, tie a second knot over it.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:3
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Twist the stick until bleeding stops.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:4
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: The person will feel severe pain this is expected and normal.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:5
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: SECURE: Tie the stick in place so it cannot unwind.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:6
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: RECORD TIME: Write the time of application on the person's forehead or arm with a pen, marker, or anything available.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:7
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Tell EMS when it was applied.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:8
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: DO NOT REMOVE: Only trained medical personnel should remove a tourniquet.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:9
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Embedded Objects [Page 11] (cid:127) If an object (knife, glass, debris) is embedded in the wound DO NOT remove it.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:10
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: It may be stemming blood flow.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:11
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Pad around it to stabilise it in place without pressing on it.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:12
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Ongoing Care Monitor pulse every few minutes.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:13
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Signs of worsening shock (pale, cold, confused) require EMS urgently.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:14
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Keep the person lying flat with legs elevated unless injury prevents it.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:15
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: n WHAT NOT TO DO Do NOT remove a blood-soaked dressing this disrupts the clot forming underneath.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:16
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Do NOT use a tourniquet on the neck, chest, abdomen, or groin limbs only.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:17
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Do NOT remove an embedded object.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:18
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Do NOT apply a tourniquet using wire, rope, or thin cord they cause tissue damage without stopping bleeding.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:19
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: When to Call EMS (cid:127) Bleeding cannot be controlled with 10 minutes of direct pressure (cid:127) Spurting arterial bleeding (cid:127) Deep wounds with visible tissue, tendon, muscle, or bone (cid:127) Any signs of shock develop (cid:127) Wound is on the head, neck, chest, abdomen, or groin [Page 12] 6 SUSPECTED FRACTURES & SPRAINS A fracture is a break in a bone.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:20
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: A sprain is a tear or stretch of ligaments around a joint.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:21
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Without imaging, it is often impossible to distinguish between them in the field.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:22
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Treat any suspected fracture as confirmed.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:23
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Open fractures (bone visible) carry serious infection risk and require urgent medical attention.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:24
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Mishandling a fracture especially of the spine can cause permanent paralysis.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:25
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Signs & Symptoms (cid:127) Both fracture and sprain: Pain, swelling, bruising at the injury site (cid:127) Fracture-specific: Deformity limb looks bent, shortened, or out of position (cid:127) Grinding or grating sensation when moved (do not test deliberately) (cid:127) Complete inability or

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:0
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: fracture especially of the spine can cause permanent paralysis.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:1
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Signs & Symptoms (cid:127) Both fracture and sprain: Pain, swelling, bruising at the injury site (cid:127) Fracture-specific: Deformity limb looks bent, shortened, or out of position (cid:127) Grinding or grating sensation when moved (do not test deliberately) (cid:127) Complete inability or strong refusal to use or bear weight on the limb (cid:127) Bone visibly protruding through the skin (open/compound fracture) (cid:127) Numbness or tingling below the injury (nerve involvement) Immediate Actions 1.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:2
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: STOP ALL MOVEMENT: Tell the person to stay still.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:3
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Do not try to straighten the limb.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:4
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: CONTROL BLEEDING: If there is an open wound apply gentle direct pressure around (not on) the wound.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:5
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Do not push exposed bone back in.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:6
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: SPLINT IN PLACE: Immobilise the limb in the position you find it.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:7
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Use any rigid material alongside it a folded newspaper, rolled clothing, or sticks.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:8
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Tie above AND below the fracture site not over it.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:9
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: PAD THE SPLINT: Add soft padding between the rigid splint and the limb for comfort.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:10
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: CHECK CIRCULATION: After splinting feel that fingers or toes below the fracture are warm.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:11
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Can the person feel you touching them?

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:12
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: If cold, pale, or numb the splint is too tight.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:13
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: ELEVATE: If possible, rest the injured limb elevated above heart level to reduce swelling.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:14
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: COVER OPEN FRACTURES: If bone is visible, cover loosely with a clean, damp cloth.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:15
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Do not attempt to push bone back.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:16
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: This is a high infection risk.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:17
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: ICE (if available): Apply a cold pack or ice wrapped in cloth for 20 minutes to reduce swelling.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:18
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Never apply ice directly to skin.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:19
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Suspected Spinal Injury CRITICAL CAUTION n DO NOT MOVE A PERSON WITH A SUSPECTED SPINAL INJURY.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:20
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Suspect spinal injury after: high-speed accident, fall from height, diving injury, or any trauma with neck pain, back pain, or tingling/numbness in limbs.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:21
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Keep the head and neck perfectly still.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:22
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Do not allow the person to sit up.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:23
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Only move if the scene becomes life-threatening and you have no other option.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:24
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: If you must move them keep the head, neck, and spine aligned in a straight line at all times.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:25
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Ongoing Care Keep the person still and warm.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:26
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Re-check circulation distal to the splint every 10 minutes.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:27
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Do not give food or water if surgery may be needed.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:28
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Reassure and monitor for signs of shock.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11:0
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: head, neck, and spine aligned in a straight line at all times.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11:1
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Ongoing Care Keep the person still and warm.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11:2
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Re-check circulation distal to the splint every 10 minutes.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11:3
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Do not give food or water if surgery may be needed.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11:4
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Reassure and monitor for signs of shock.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11:5
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: [Page 13] n WHAT NOT TO DO Do NOT attempt to realign, straighten, or 'reset' a fractured limb.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11:6
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Do NOT apply ice directly to skin wrap it first.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11:7
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11
s: First_Aid_Guide
t: Do NOT move a person with suspected spinal injury unless their life is in immediate danger.

i: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11:8
c: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11
